common_name: Alta Magnolia (Narrow Columnar Southern Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Alta is a narrow, tightly columnar southern magnolia bred for improved cold hardiness and small-space use.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Alta bears the classic large, creamy-white, lemon-scented southern magnolia blooms and glossy evergreen foliage on an unusually narrow, densely branched, columnar form that fits tight side yards, screens, and formal allees where a full-spreading southern magnolia would be too wide. Its improved cold hardiness compared to many older cultivars extends its usable range further north than the species is typically recommended. Water deeply during establishment, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune only to remove dead or damaged wood, since magnolias need little routine pruning.

common_name: Brozzonii Magnolia (Very Large Nearly-White Late-Blooming Saucer Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Brozzonii is a late-blooming saucer magnolia cultivar whose delayed flowering helps its enormous blooms dodge late frost damage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Brozzonii produces some of the largest flowers of any saucer magnolia cultivar, goblet-shaped and nearly white with only a faint pink flush at the base, opening on bare branches before the leaves emerge. It blooms noticeably later than 'Alexandrina' and most other saucer magnolias, a valuable trait that lets its flowers largely escape the late hard freezes that regularly damage earlier-opening cultivars. The tree grows into a broad, multi-stemmed small tree with minimal pruning needs beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Verbanica Magnolia (Late-Blooming Rosy-Pink Saucer Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Verbanica is a late-blooming saucer magnolia with rosy-pink cupped flowers and coppery fall foliage color.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Verbanica bears cup-shaped, rosy-pink flowers with a paler interior, opening later in spring than most saucer magnolia cultivars, which lets its blooms largely escape the late hard freezes that damage earlier-flowering selections. The foliage turns an attractive coppery-bronze in fall, adding a second season of interest beyond the spring bloom. The tree grows into a broad, multi-stemmed small tree with minimal pruning needs beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Waterlily Star Magnolia (Pale Pink Many-Petaled Star Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped plants in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Waterlily is a star magnolia cultivar with an unusually high petal count opening from silvery-pink buds.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Waterlily opens from soft silvery-pink buds into fragrant, nearly ice-white flowers with up to 25 narrow, strap-like tepals, a fuller flower form reminiscent of a waterlily bloom that has made it one of the most sought-after star magnolia selections. Like other star magnolias it flowers on bare branches in late winter to early spring before any foliage appears, creating a striking floral display, though the early bloom timing can leave flowers vulnerable to browning from a late hard freeze. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Centennial Star Magnolia (Arnold Arboretum Pure White Star Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped plants in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Centennial was released by the Arnold Arboretum in 1972 to mark its hundredth anniversary.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Centennial, introduced by the Arnold Arboretum in 1972 for its hundredth anniversary, bears pure white, fragrant, star-shaped flowers with 28 to 33 narrow tepals per bloom, a notably high petal count that gives an exceptionally full, showy floral display in late winter to early spring before the leaves emerge. It grows a bit more vigorously and upright than many other star magnolia selections, developing into a small tree over time rather than staying strictly shrubby. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Jane Platt Magnolia (Double Fragrant Pink Star Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped plants in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Jane Platt is widely regarded as one of the best pink-flowered star magnolia selections.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Jane Platt bears fragrant, soft pale-pink, double flowers with 20 to 30 narrow tepals per bloom, opening on bare branches in late winter to early spring before the leaves emerge and considered by many magnolia growers to be the finest pink star magnolia available. Its slow growth and naturally compact, shrubby habit suit it well to smaller gardens where a full-sized flowering tree would be impractical. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Rosea Star Magnolia (Pink-Flushed Star Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped plants in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Rosea is a classic pink-toned star magnolia selection, its buds flushed with pink fading to near-white as they open.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Rosea opens from pink-flushed buds into star-shaped flowers that fade to a soft near-white as they mature, giving the bloom a two-toned effect across the flowering period in late winter to early spring before the leaves emerge. It is one of the older and more widely available pink-toned star magnolia cultivars, with the same fine-textured, multi-tepaled flower form and light fragrance typical of the species. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Nigra Lily Magnolia (Deep Purple-Red Tulip Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Nigra bears deep purple-red, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact shrub that sporadically reblooms into summer and fall.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Nigra bears narrow, upright, tulip-shaped flowers in the deepest purple-red of any commonly grown lily magnolia cultivar, opening in mid-spring as the leaves begin to emerge and continuing sporadically through summer into fall, an unusual and valuable trait among flowering magnolias. Its compact, shrubby habit tops out smaller than the tree-form magnolias, making it a good fit for foundation plantings or a mixed shrub border. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune lightly after the main spring flush to shape.

common_name: O'Neill Lily Magnolia (Red-Purple Veined Tulip Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; O'Neill bears rich red-purple, pink-veined tulip-shaped flowers on a compact shrub.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. O'Neill bears upright, tulip-shaped flowers in rich red-purple on the outside with a pink-veined interior, each with seven to nine tepals, opening in mid-spring as the leaves begin to emerge on a compact, shrubby plant. Its full, richly colored flowers and manageable size make it a good choice for a foundation planting or mixed shrub border where a full-sized flowering tree magnolia would be too large. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune lightly after the main spring flush to shape.

common_name: Judy Magnolia (Little Girl Series Reddish-Purple Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Judy is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred for later, frost-dodging bloom on a compact, upright plant.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Judy is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later bloom timing that helps the flowers dodge late spring frosts, producing reddish-purple, tulip-shaped blooms on a vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed plant. Its later flowering window gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

common_name: Pinkie Magnolia (Little Girl Series Fuchsia-to-Pale-Pink Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Pinkie is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred for later, frost-dodging bloom on a compact, upright plant.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Pinkie is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later bloom timing, producing tulip-shaped flowers colored deep fuchsia-pink at the base fading to pale pink at the tips, with a white interior, on a compact, multi-stemmed plant. Its later flowering window gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

common_name: Randy Magnolia (Little Girl Series Deep Purple-Red Vigorous Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Randy is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias, notably vigorous and upright, bred for later, frost-dodging bloom.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Randy is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later bloom timing, producing deep purple-red, tulip-shaped flowers on a notably vigorous, upright plant that grows larger than most of its Little Girl siblings. Its later flowering window gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

common_name: Ricki Magnolia (Little Girl Series Large-Flowered Deep Pink Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Ricki is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias, noted for its unusually large flowers, bred for later, frost-dodging bloom.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Ricki is one of the eight 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolias bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for later bloom timing, producing unusually large, deep purple-pink, tulip-shaped flowers on a compact, multi-stemmed plant. Its later flowering window gives it a significant advantage over earlier magnolias in regions with unpredictable late frosts, and its larger bloom size stands out among its Little Girl siblings. Water regularly during establishment, mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune minimally beyond removing damaged or crossing branches.

common_name: Cherokee Sunset Flowering Dogwood (Variegated Pink-Bracted Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Cherokee Sunset bears variegated pink, green, and yellow foliage along with pink bracts.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; understory planting beneath high, open tree canopy mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. Cherokee Sunset bears striking variegated foliage in shades of pink, green, and cream through the growing season, turning deep purple-red in fall, complementing a spring display of pink flower bracts and paired with the good mildew and anthracnose resistance bred into the Cherokee series of dogwood cultivars. Its combination of colorful foliage and floral display gives it two strong seasons of interest beyond the standard white or pink dogwood bloom alone. Water during dry spells, especially the first two years, and avoid deep planting or heavy mulch piled against the trunk.

common_name: Cherokee Daybreak Flowering Dogwood (White-Edged Variegated Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Cherokee Daybreak bears creamy-white-edged variegated foliage along with white flower bracts.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; understory planting beneath high, open tree canopy mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. Cherokee Daybreak bears green leaves edged in creamy white through the growing season, brightening the canopy from a distance, and pairs the variegation with a heavy spring display of white flower bracts and rich pink-to-deep-red fall color. Its bright, variegated foliage gives it strong ornamental value even when not in bloom. Water during dry spells, especially the first two years, and avoid deep planting or heavy mulch piled against the trunk.

common_name: First Lady Flowering Dogwood (Yellow-Variegated Fall-Color Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; First Lady bears yellow-variegated foliage that turns red and maroon in autumn.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; understory planting beneath high, open tree canopy mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. First Lady bears foliage marked with bright yellow variegation through spring and summer, transitioning to vivid red and maroon fall color, giving the tree strong ornamental value well beyond its white spring flower bract display. Its bright variegated leaves stand out against darker-foliaged plantings and make it a good specimen or focal accent. Water during dry spells, especially the first two years, and avoid deep planting or heavy mulch piled against the trunk.

common_name: Plena Flowering Dogwood (Double-Bracted White Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Plena bears an unusual double set of white bracts giving each bloom a fuller, rose-like appearance.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; understory planting beneath high, open tree canopy mimics its native woodland-edge habitat best. Plena bears an unusual double layer of white bracts, up to eight per bloom rather than the typical four, giving each flower a fuller, rose-like appearance that sets it apart from standard flowering dogwoods, along with good resistance to anthracnose. Its distinctive double-bracted form has made it a favorite among collectors seeking something beyond the common dogwood look. Water during dry spells, especially the first two years, and avoid deep planting or heavy mulch piled against the trunk.

common_name: Little Poncho Kousa Dogwood (Dwarf Heavy-Flowering Kousa Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Little Poncho is a dwarf kousa dogwood reaching only 8 to 10 feet, well suited to small gardens.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Little Poncho stays notably compact for a kousa dogwood, reaching only about eight to ten feet at maturity, yet blooms as heavily as full-sized cultivars, covering itself with creamy-white, four-bracted flowers in early summer despite its small stature. Its diminutive size makes it one of the few kousa dogwoods practical for a small urban lot or foundation planting. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Samaritan Kousa Dogwood (White-Margined Variegated Kousa Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; Samaritan bears white-margined variegated foliage and a showy display of white bracts, and benefits from some afternoon shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure that can scorch the variegated leaves. Samaritan bears leaves boldly margined in creamy white around a green center, paired with a heavy early-summer display of showy white bracts, giving the tree strong ornamental appeal both in and out of bloom. Its variegated foliage brightens shaded plantings and provides contrast against darker-leaved companion shrubs. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Greensleeves Kousa Dogwood (Heavy-Flowering Fast-Growing Kousa Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Greensleeves is a heavy-flowering, comparatively fast-growing kousa dogwood cultivar with excellent red fall color.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Greensleeves bears dark, prominently veined foliage and grows faster than many other kousa dogwood selections, flowering heavily and reliably from a young age with showy white bracts in early summer, followed by excellent red fall color. Its combination of vigor and dependable flowering has made it a popular choice where a quicker-establishing kousa dogwood is wanted. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Empire Kousa Dogwood (Compact Upright Rutgers Kousa Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Empire is a Rutgers-bred kousa dogwood with a compact, upright habit and reliably heavy flowering.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Empire, bred at Rutgers University, grows in a compact, upright form narrower than the species, making it a good fit for smaller landscapes or where space is limited, while still producing a heavy, reliable early-summer display of white bracts. Its tidy habit requires less pruning to maintain a neat form than more spreading kousa dogwood cultivars. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after flowering.

common_name: Hearts of Gold Redbud (Golden-Yellow Foliage Redbud)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Hearts of Gold is grown chiefly for its bright golden-yellow summer foliage, emerging reddish-orange in spring.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; some afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch on the bright foliage in the hottest part of the Gulf South. Hearts of Gold is prized chiefly for its striking heart-shaped foliage, emerging reddish-orange in spring and maturing to a bright, glowing golden-yellow that holds color through summer before deepening toward green, a dramatic foliage display that follows the classic rosy-pink spring flowers typical of the species. Its bold color makes it a strong focal point in a mixed border or woodland-edge planting. Redbud roots are susceptible to rot in wet, poorly drained sites, so ensure adequate drainage, and prune minimally beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Flame Redbud (Double-Flowered Seedless Pink Redbud)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Flame bears unusual double pink flowers on an upright tree that sets very few seed pods.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Flame bears unusual double, rosy-pink flowers that create a fuller, more ruffled bloom than the typical single-flowered redbud, opening on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, and it produces very few seed pods, an advantage for gardeners who find the abundant pods of standard redbuds messy. The upright tree carries the classic heart-shaped summer foliage and yellow fall color typical of the species. Redbud roots are susceptible to rot in wet, poorly drained sites, so ensure adequate drainage, and prune minimally beyond removing dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Pink Chimes Japanese Snowbell (Pale Pink-Flowered Snowbell Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pink Chimes bears pale pink-flushed flowers on a broad, rounded small tree, and does not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally as an understory tree beneath high-canopy shade; Japanese snowbell is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Pink Chimes bears pendant, bell-shaped flowers softly flushed with pale pink rather than the pure white of the species, hanging in rows beneath the horizontal branching in late spring to early summer for the same elegant, layered floral display Japanese snowbell is known for. Its subtle pink coloring adds a gentler tone to the classic snowbell look, particularly appealing planted where the pendant blooms can be viewed from below. Mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches, since the tree's natural layered form needs little shaping.

common_name: Emerald Pagoda Japanese Snowbell (Large-Flowered Vigorous Snowbell Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Emerald Pagoda bears unusually large white flowers and thicker, more vigorous foliage than the species, and does not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally as an understory tree beneath high-canopy shade; Japanese snowbell is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Emerald Pagoda bears noticeably larger, pure white, pendant, bell-shaped flowers than the species type, held above thicker, glossier, more substantial foliage on a more vigorous, upright-growing tree that establishes faster than many other snowbell selections. Its larger flowers and stronger growth make it a good choice where a bolder, quicker-maturing specimen is wanted. Mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches.

common_name: Carillon Japanese Snowbell (Weeping White-Flowered Snowbell Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or large shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Carillon is a weeping, pendulous-form Japanese snowbell suited to smaller gardens, and does not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally as an understory planting beneath high-canopy shade; Japanese snowbell is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Carillon grows in a distinctly weeping, pendulous form, its cascading branches hung with white, bell-shaped flowers in late spring to early summer, forming a broad, shrubby mound rather than the upright tree shape typical of the species. Its smaller, weeping habit suits a spot where a full-sized snowbell tree would be too large, such as near a patio or at the front of a shaded border. Mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches.

common_name: Fragrant Fountain Japanese Snowbell (Strongly Weeping Fragrant Snowbell Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or large shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Fragrant Fountain is a strongly weeping Japanese snowbell with fragrant white flowers, and does not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, ideally as an understory planting beneath high-canopy shade; Japanese snowbell is intolerant of drought, alkaline soils, and compacted sites. Fragrant Fountain cascades even more strongly than other weeping snowbell selections, its pendulous branches dripping with fragrant, white, bell-shaped flowers in late spring to early summer, forming a low, mounded, fountain-like silhouette. Its pronounced weeping form and noticeable fragrance make it a strong specimen near a patio, entry, or water feature where its scent and cascading habit can both be appreciated up close. Mulch to keep the root zone cool and moist, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches.

common_name: Emerald Knight Fringe Tree (Fruitless Male Native Fringe Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Emerald Knight is a male (fruitless) native fringe tree selection with an upright, dense habit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; native fringe tree tolerates a wide range of soils once established and is a tough, low-maintenance small flowering tree for the Southeast. Emerald Knight is a male selection of the native fringe tree bred for an upright, dense habit and glossy dark-green foliage, and being male it sets no fruit, avoiding the dropped-fruit litter of female or seed-grown plants while still producing the species' signature cloud of fragrant, fringe-like white flowers in mid-spring. Its denser, more structured form than typical seedling fringe trees suits it well to formal plantings or as a specimen near a patio. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood, since fringe tree needs little routine pruning.
